q: What is a computer network?
a: A computer network is a group of connected devices that communicate and share data or resources through wired or wireless connections.
why: A network does not need internet access to exist.

q: What is the OSI model?
a: The Open Systems Interconnection model is a seven-layer reference model that explains how network communication functions are organized.
why: The OSI model is conceptual; actual networks commonly use the TCP/IP protocol suite.

q: What does OSI Layer 1 do?
a: The Physical layer transmits raw bits over physical media using electrical, optical, or radio signals.
why: Cables, connectors, signaling, and physical link problems relate to Layer 1.

q: What does OSI Layer 2 do?
a: The Data Link layer handles framing, local link delivery, and MAC addressing on technologies such as Ethernet.
why: Ethernet switches primarily make forwarding decisions at Layer 2.

q: What does OSI Layer 3 do?
a: The Network layer provides logical addressing and routing so packets can travel between different IP networks.
why: IP addresses and routers are closely associated with Layer 3.

q: What does OSI Layer 4 do?
a: The Transport layer provides end-to-end communication services using protocols such as TCP and UDP.
why: TCP and UDP port numbers help identify application endpoints.

q: What does OSI Layer 5 do?
a: The Session layer describes functions for establishing, managing, and ending communication sessions between applications.
why: TCP/IP implementations do not generally use a separate Session layer.

q: What does OSI Layer 6 do?
a: The Presentation layer describes data representation, translation, compression, and encryption-related functions.
why: Encryption is not performed exclusively at OSI Layer 6.

q: What does OSI Layer 7 do?
a: The Application layer provides network services to applications through protocols such as HTTP, DNS, and SMTP.
why: Layer 7 refers to application protocols, not the physical application window.

q: What is encapsulation?
a: Encapsulation is the process of adding protocol headers and sometimes trailers as data moves down the networking layers for transmission.
why: The receiving device processes the corresponding information through decapsulation.

q: Which OSI layer uses Ethernet frames?
a: Layer 2, the Data Link layer, uses frames to carry data across an Ethernet link.
why: An IP packet can be carried inside an Ethernet frame.

q: What are the data units at Layers 1, 2, and 3?
a: Layer 1 carries bits, Layer 2 uses frames, and Layer 3 uses packets.
why: Transport-layer data units include TCP segments and UDP datagrams.

q: What is the TCP/IP model?
a: The TCP/IP model organizes internet communication into Link, Internet, Transport, and Application layers.
why: Some textbooks use a five-layer variation that separates Physical and Data Link.

q: What is the difference between TCP and UDP?
a: TCP provides reliable, ordered byte-stream delivery using acknowledgments and retransmission. UDP sends independent datagrams without guaranteeing delivery or order.
why: UDP is not automatically faster in every application.

q: What are the three steps of the TCP handshake?
a: A client sends SYN, the server replies SYN-ACK, and the client responds with ACK.
why: The handshake establishes the TCP connection before normal data transfer.

q: What is a LAN?
a: A Local Area Network connects devices within a limited area such as a home, school, office, or campus.
why: A LAN can contain multiple VLANs and IP subnets.

q: What is a WAN?
a: A Wide Area Network connects networks across geographically separated locations.
why: A WAN may be private and does not necessarily mean the public internet.

q: What is the difference between bandwidth and throughput?
a: Bandwidth describes a link's nominal capacity, while throughput is the actual rate of successful data transfer.
why: Congestion, overhead, and errors can reduce throughput below the link's bandwidth.

q: What is network latency?
a: Latency is the time taken for data to travel from one point to another, usually measured in milliseconds.
why: Ping commonly reports round-trip time rather than one-way latency.

q: What is a Layer 2 switch?
a: A Layer 2 switch connects Ethernet devices and forwards frames using destination MAC addresses and a learned MAC address table.
why: A Layer 2 switch does not normally route IP packets between VLANs.
imgAlt: Real Cisco Catalyst Ethernet switch ports

q: How does a switch learn MAC addresses?
a: A switch reads the source MAC address of an incoming Ethernet frame and records its association with the receiving port and VLAN.
why: Learning uses the source MAC; forwarding decisions use the destination MAC.
imgAlt: Real Cisco Catalyst Ethernet switch ports

q: What happens when a switch knows the destination MAC address?
a: For a known unicast destination on another port, the switch forwards the frame through the associated port.
why: The destination MAC lookup is performed in the relevant VLAN.

q: What happens to an unknown unicast Ethernet frame?
a: A switch normally floods an unknown unicast frame to eligible forwarding ports in the same VLAN, excluding the ingress port.
why: Flooding is generally limited to the VLAN and forwarding topology.

q: What does a switch do with a broadcast frame?
a: A switch normally floods a broadcast frame through eligible forwarding ports in the same VLAN except the port that received it.
why: Routers do not normally forward Layer 2 broadcasts between subnets.

q: What is the Ethernet broadcast MAC address?
a: The Ethernet broadcast destination address is FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF.
why: All six octets contain hexadecimal FF.

q: What is the purpose of the MAC address table?
a: It maps learned MAC addresses and VLANs to switch ports so the switch can forward frames efficiently.
why: Dynamic MAC entries normally age out after a period of inactivity.

q: What is a common default MAC aging time on Cisco switches?
a: Many Cisco Catalyst switches use a default dynamic MAC aging time of 300 seconds, although the value is platform-dependent and configurable.
why: Do not assume every switch platform uses exactly 300 seconds.

q: What is an Ethernet frame?
a: An Ethernet frame is a Layer 2 data unit containing destination and source MAC addresses, a type or length field, payload, and an error-detection field.
why: The Frame Check Sequence helps detect corrupted frames.

q: What does an Ethernet FCS error indicate?
a: An FCS error indicates that a received Ethernet frame failed its integrity check, potentially because of corruption or a link problem.
why: Inspect physical media and interface counters before assuming the application is responsible.

q: What is a duplex mismatch?
a: A duplex mismatch occurs when linked devices operate with incompatible half-duplex and full-duplex settings.
why: It can cause poor throughput, late collisions, and frame errors.

q: What is the typical maximum length of a copper Ethernet channel using 1000BASE-T?
a: A standards-compliant 1000BASE-T twisted-pair channel supports up to 100 meters under specified cabling conditions.
why: The horizontal permanent link is typically limited to 90 meters, with patch cords making up the remainder.

q: What does PoE provide?
a: Power over Ethernet supplies electrical power and network data over compatible Ethernet cabling.
why: Common PoE devices include access points, IP phones, and network cameras.

q: What is CDP?
a: Cisco Discovery Protocol is a Cisco neighbor-discovery protocol that advertises information about directly connected devices.
why: CDP is Cisco-specific and should be evaluated against the organization's discovery-policy requirements.

q: What is LLDP?
a: Link Layer Discovery Protocol is a vendor-neutral Layer 2 protocol for discovering directly connected network devices.
why: LLDP is useful when validating connections involving multiple vendors.

q: What is Spanning Tree Protocol?
a: Spanning Tree Protocol prevents Layer 2 forwarding loops by controlling which redundant paths forward traffic.
why: Redundant physical links can remain connected without all of them forwarding simultaneously.

q: How is the STP root bridge selected?
a: The bridge with the lowest Bridge ID becomes the root; the Bridge ID includes priority-related information and a MAC address.
why: Lower priority wins before the MAC address is used as a tie-breaker.

q: What is an STP root port?
a: A root port is a nonroot bridge's selected port offering its best path toward the root bridge.
why: The root bridge itself has no root port.

q: What does a Rapid STP alternate port provide?
a: An alternate port provides an alternate path toward the root bridge and normally remains in the discarding state until needed.
why: An alternate port is not normally forwarding user data.

q: What does PortFast do?
a: PortFast allows an appropriate edge port to transition rapidly to forwarding without waiting through traditional STP convergence.
why: Use PortFast on appropriate edge links, not indiscriminately on switch-to-switch links.

q: What happens when BPDU Guard receives a BPDU on a protected port?
a: On typical Cisco IOS configurations, BPDU Guard places the port into an error-disabled state when a BPDU is received.
why: BPDU Guard is designed to protect edge connections from unexpected bridging devices.

q: What is the purpose of Root Guard?
a: Root Guard prevents a designated port from accepting a superior BPDU that would otherwise change the STP root relationship.
why: A protected port enters a root-inconsistent condition while superior BPDUs continue.

q: What is the purpose of Loop Guard?
a: Loop Guard helps prevent a blocked or alternate STP port from incorrectly becoming designated when expected BPDUs stop arriving.
why: Loop Guard and Root Guard protect against different spanning-tree failure conditions.

q: What is EtherChannel?
a: EtherChannel combines multiple compatible physical Ethernet links into one logical port-channel interface.
why: Member ports must have compatible settings for successful bundling.

q: What is LACP?
a: Link Aggregation Control Protocol negotiates and manages compatible Ethernet links within a logical link aggregation group.
cli:
interface range GigabitEthernet0/1 - 2
channel-group 1 mode active
why: LACP active can negotiate with active or passive; passive-passive does not initiate a bundle.

q: Which command summarizes EtherChannel member status?
a: The show etherchannel summary command displays port-channel groups, protocol indicators, and member-port status.
why: A bundled port marked P is not the same as a suspended or standalone port.

q: What is a VLAN?
a: A Virtual LAN logically separates Layer 2 devices into distinct broadcast domains.
why: Different VLANs require Layer 3 forwarding to exchange IP traffic.

q: What is an access port?
a: An access port normally carries traffic for one data VLAN and sends or receives ordinary endpoint Ethernet frames without 802.1Q data-VLAN tags.
why: Voice VLAN configurations can also support tagged voice traffic on the same edge link.

q: Which commands assign an access port to VLAN 10?
a: Set the interface to access mode and assign its access VLAN to 10.
cli:
vlan 10
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
switchport mode access
switchport access vlan 10
why: Check that the VLAN exists and the interface is operational.

q: What is an 802.1Q trunk?
a: An 802.1Q trunk carries traffic for multiple VLANs across one Ethernet link using VLAN identification tags for tagged traffic.
why: The native VLAN is normally transmitted untagged on a Cisco 802.1Q trunk.

q: Which command configures a switchport as a trunk on supported Cisco switches?
a: Use switchport mode trunk under the interface configuration.
why: On platforms that require encapsulation selection, configure 802.1Q first.

q: What is a native VLAN?
a: The native VLAN is the VLAN associated with untagged traffic received on an 802.1Q trunk.
why: A native-VLAN mismatch can cause unexpected connectivity and security problems.

q: Which command restricts a trunk to VLANs 10 and 20?
a: Use switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20 on the trunk interface.
cli:
interface GigabitEthernet0/24
switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20
why: An allowed VLAN must also exist and be operational for traffic to pass.

q: What is a voice VLAN?
a: A voice VLAN provides a separate logical network for compatible IP-phone voice traffic on a switch edge port.
cli:
interface GigabitEthernet0/5
switchport mode access
switchport access vlan 10
switchport voice vlan 20
why: A connected PC may use the data VLAN while the phone uses the voice VLAN.

q: What is inter-VLAN routing?
a: Inter-VLAN routing forwards IP packets between different VLAN networks using a router or Layer 3 switch.
why: Switching within one VLAN does not automatically provide connectivity to another VLAN.

q: What is router-on-a-stick?
a: Router-on-a-stick uses one router physical interface with multiple tagged subinterfaces to route between VLANs over a trunk.
cli:
interface GigabitEthernet0/0.10
encapsulation dot1Q 10
ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
why: Each routed VLAN typically has a separate router subinterface and IP subnet.

q: What is a switch virtual interface?
a: An SVI is a logical Layer 3 interface associated with a VLAN, used for management or inter-VLAN routing on capable switches.
cli:
interface Vlan10
ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
no shutdown
why: An SVI may remain down without an eligible active Layer 2 port in its VLAN.

q: Which command enables IPv4 routing on a Cisco multilayer switch?
a: The global configuration command ip routing enables IPv4 packet routing on supported Layer 3 switches.
why: Giving an SVI an address alone does not necessarily enable routing between VLANs.

q: What does show vlan brief display?
a: It lists VLAN IDs, names, status, and associated access ports.
why: Use show interfaces trunk to inspect operational trunks.

q: Which command verifies operational trunk ports?
a: The show interfaces trunk command displays trunk status, native VLANs, and allowed VLAN information.
why: A configured trunk does not always mean the link is operational.

q: What is the default VLAN on many Cisco Catalyst switches?
a: VLAN 1 is the default VLAN on many Cisco Catalyst platforms.
why: Production designs commonly separate user, management, and native-VLAN functions.

q: What is DTP?
a: Dynamic Trunking Protocol is a Cisco protocol that can negotiate trunk operation between compatible switch ports.
why: Explicitly configured ports reduce unintended trunk negotiation.

q: What does switchport nonegotiate do?
a: It disables DTP negotiation on supported switch interfaces without itself determining whether the port is an access port or trunk.
why: Both ends must be configured compatibly when negotiation is disabled.

q: What happens when two PCs have different VLAN IDs but the same IPv4 subnet configured?
a: They remain in separate Layer 2 broadcast domains and normally cannot communicate directly using ordinary ARP and switching alone.
why: An identical subnet mask does not override VLAN separation.

q: What is a routed switch port?
a: A routed port operates as a Layer 3 interface rather than as a switchport assigned to a VLAN.
cli:
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
no switchport
ip address 10.0.0.1 255.255.255.252
why: Routed ports do not use normal access-VLAN or trunk configuration.

q: What is an IPv4 address?
a: An IPv4 address is a 32-bit logical address used to identify an interface within an IPv4 network.
why: IPv4 addresses are commonly written as four decimal octets.

q: What is a subnet mask?
a: A subnet mask identifies the network-prefix bits and host bits of an IPv4 address.
why: A valid conventional IPv4 subnet mask has contiguous one bits followed by zero bits.

q: What is subnetting?
a: Subnetting divides a larger IP network into smaller logical networks using longer network prefixes.
why: Subnet boundaries are determined by the prefix length or subnet mask.

q: What does CIDR mean?
a: Classless Inter-Domain Routing uses variable-length network prefixes for address allocation and routing instead of fixed address classes.
why: The /24 notation specifies a 24-bit network prefix.

q: What subnet mask corresponds to /26?
a: A /26 IPv4 prefix corresponds to subnet mask 255.255.255.192.
why: The prefix uses 26 network bits and leaves 6 host bits.

q: Which subnet contains 192.168.1.70/26?
a: The address belongs to 192.168.1.64/26, covering addresses 192.168.1.64 through 192.168.1.127.
why: A /26 creates blocks of 64 addresses in the final octet.

q: What is the broadcast address of 192.168.1.70/26?
a: The directed broadcast address is 192.168.1.127.
why: For a conventional IPv4 subnet, the broadcast is its final address.

q: How many usable host addresses are in a conventional /26 subnet?
a: A /26 has 64 total addresses and 62 conventional usable host addresses.
why: The network and directed-broadcast addresses are reserved.

q: How many usable host addresses are in a conventional /27 subnet?
a: A /27 has 32 total addresses and 30 conventional usable host addresses.
why: Use 2^(32 minus prefix length), then subtract two for conventional subnets.

q: What is the block size for the mask 255.255.255.224?
a: The increment in the last octet is 32, calculated as 256 minus 224.
why: The subnet network addresses occur at multiples of 32.

q: Which /27 subnet contains 192.168.10.45?
a: The address belongs to 192.168.10.32/27, whose range ends at 192.168.10.63.
why: A /27 increments by 32 in the last octet.

q: How many conventional usable host addresses does a /30 have?
a: A /30 contains four addresses: one network, two usable host addresses, and one broadcast.
why: /30 is commonly used for small point-to-point IPv4 links.

q: Why is /31 useful on point-to-point links?
a: RFC 3021 allows both addresses of a /31 IPv4 prefix to be used on supported point-to-point links.
why: Do not apply the conventional subtract-two rule to a supported /31 point-to-point link.

q: What is a /32 IPv4 prefix?
a: A /32 identifies exactly one IPv4 address and is commonly used for host routes and loopback addresses.
why: /32 is not a conventional multi-host subnet.

q: What are the RFC 1918 private IPv4 ranges?
why: Not every address starting with 172 is private.

q: What is an APIPA IPv4 address?
a: An APIPA address is an automatically selected IPv4 link-local address in 169.254.0.0/16 when suitable automatic configuration is unavailable.
why: An unexpected 169.254 address often suggests a DHCP problem.

q: What is a default gateway?
a: A default gateway is the next-hop router a host normally uses to reach destinations outside its directly connected network.
why: A wrong gateway can break remote connectivity while local communication still works.
imgAlt: Original technical diagram for Network Basics

q: What does ARP do?
a: Address Resolution Protocol resolves an IPv4 address to a Layer 2 MAC address on an Ethernet-style local network.
why: For a remote destination, the sender usually resolves the next-hop gateway's MAC.

q: Does a host ARP for a remote server's MAC address?
a: Normally no. It ARPs for the local next hop, usually its default gateway, and sends the remote IP packet inside that local Ethernet frame.
why: Layer 2 destination addresses can change at each routed hop.

q: What is VLSM?
a: Variable Length Subnet Masking assigns different prefix lengths to different subnets to match their address requirements.
why: Allocate larger required subnets first when designing an address plan.

q: What is the network address of 192.168.5.200/25?
a: The network address is 192.168.5.128 because /25 divides the last octet into 0–127 and 128–255.
why: The last octet is 200, so it falls in the second /25 block.

q: What is a wildcard mask?
a: A wildcard mask identifies which IPv4 address bits must match and which bits may vary in Cisco ACLs and certain routing configurations.
why: For an ordinary inverse subnet mask, subtract each mask octet from 255.

q: What wildcard mask corresponds to a /24 subnet?
a: The wildcard mask for 255.255.255.0 is 0.0.0.255.
why: Zero means match the bit; one means the bit is ignored.

q: What is the purpose of ping?
a: Ping tests IP reachability and measures response timing using ICMP Echo Request and Echo Reply messages when permitted.
why: A failed ping does not prove the remote device is offline because ICMP may be filtered.

q: How long is an IPv6 address?
a: An IPv6 address contains 128 bits and is normally represented using hexadecimal groups separated by colons.
why: IPv6 addresses are four times as long in bits as IPv4 addresses.

q: What does :: mean in an IPv6 address?
a: A double colon compresses one consecutive sequence of all-zero 16-bit groups within an IPv6 address.
why: Use the double-colon compression at most once in one address.

q: What is a global unicast IPv6 address?
a: A global unicast address identifies an interface in a globally routable IPv6 addressing space, subject to network routing policies.
why: The currently allocated global unicast space commonly falls within 2000::/3.

q: What is the IPv6 link-local prefix?
a: IPv6 link-local unicast addresses use FE80::/10 and are intended for communication within one link.
why: Routers do not forward link-local traffic across links.

q: What is the IPv6 unique-local address prefix?
a: IPv6 unique-local addresses occupy FC00::/7 and are generally used for local or organizational communication.
why: Locally assigned unique-local addresses normally use the FD00::/8 portion.

q: What is the IPv6 multicast prefix?
a: IPv6 multicast addresses use FF00::/8 and identify groups of receivers.
why: IPv6 uses multicast instead of a separate broadcast-address type.

q: Does IPv6 use broadcast addresses?
a: No. IPv6 uses multicast and other mechanisms for functions that IPv4 often performs with broadcasts.
why: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery uses ICMPv6 rather than ARP broadcasts.

q: What replaces ARP in IPv6?
a: IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery, an ICMPv6-based protocol suite, to resolve neighboring link-layer addresses and perform other discovery functions.
why: Neighbor Solicitation and Neighbor Advertisement are important NDP messages.

q: What is SLAAC?
a: Stateless Address Autoconfiguration allows an IPv6 host to configure addresses using information such as prefixes announced by routers.
why: Router Advertisements can supply network information without a stateful DHCPv6 address lease.

q: What is Duplicate Address Detection?
a: DAD checks whether a tentative IPv6 address is already in use on the local link.
why: DAD normally uses ICMPv6 Neighbor Solicitation.

q: What is modified EUI-64?
a: Modified EUI-64 is a method of forming a 64-bit IPv6 interface identifier from a 48-bit MAC address by inserting FFFE and inverting the universal/local bit.
why: Modern hosts may prefer stable or temporary interface identifiers instead.

q: What is the common prefix length of an IPv6 LAN subnet?
a: A /64 is the common IPv6 subnet prefix length and supports standard SLAAC interface-identifier behavior.
why: Not every IPv6 link is required to use /64, but it is the normal LAN design.

q: What is an IPv6 anycast address?
a: An anycast address is assigned to multiple interfaces, with routing delivering a packet to a reachable instance selected by the network.
why: Anycast uses unicast-format addresses rather than a separate IPv6 anycast prefix.

q: What is the IPv6 default route?
a: The IPv6 default route is ::/0, used when no more-specific matching route is available.
why: IPv6 static routes use ipv6 route rather than ip route.

q: Which Cisco command enables IPv6 unicast routing?
a: The global configuration command ipv6 unicast-routing enables IPv6 unicast packet forwarding on supported Cisco routers.
why: Interface addressing alone may not enable forwarding between IPv6 networks.

q: How do you inspect an IPv6 routing table on Cisco IOS?
a: Use show ipv6 route to display known IPv6 routing entries.
why: Check the IPv6 prefix, route source, and next-hop information.

q: Why can an IPv6 link-local next hop require an outgoing interface?
a: Link-local addresses are only unique within a link, so the outgoing interface identifies the correct scope for the next hop.
why: A next-hop FE80 address without link context may be ambiguous.

q: What is routing?
a: Routing is the process of selecting paths and forwarding Layer 3 packets toward destinations in other IP networks.
why: Routers use destination IP prefixes rather than destination MAC addresses to select network paths.

q: What is a routing table?
a: A routing table stores destination prefixes and associated forwarding information such as next hops or outgoing interfaces.
why: The most specific matching route normally determines where a packet goes.

q: What is longest prefix match?
a: Longest prefix match chooses the matching routing-table entry with the greatest number of significant network-prefix bits.
why: A matching /28 takes precedence over a matching /24 regardless of administrative distance.

q: What is administrative distance?
a: Administrative distance is a local router preference value used when selecting between routes to the same prefix learned from different sources.
why: A lower administrative distance is preferred, assuming comparable route eligibility.

q: What is a routing metric?
a: A routing metric measures route preference within a routing protocol using criteria defined by that protocol.
why: Do not compare metrics from unrelated routing protocols as though they shared one scale.

q: What does C mean in a Cisco IPv4 routing table?
a: C marks a directly connected network route.
why: A connected route normally depends on its associated interface being operational.

q: What does L mean in a Cisco IPv4 routing table?
a: L identifies a local host route for an IP address configured on the router itself.
why: For IPv4, a local interface-address route normally uses /32.

q: What does S mean in a Cisco routing table?
a: S identifies a static route configured by an administrator or management system.
why: A static route still needs a usable forwarding path before it can be installed.

q: How do you configure an IPv4 static route?
a: Use ip route followed by the destination network, subnet mask, and next-hop address or outgoing interface.
why: The specified next hop must be reachable.

q: What is the IPv4 default route?
a: The IPv4 default route is 0.0.0.0/0 and matches destinations without a more-specific route.
why: A default route is commonly used to reach an upstream router.

q: What is a floating static route?
a: A floating static route uses a higher administrative distance so it can act as a backup when the preferred route becomes unavailable.
why: Route failure detection and next-hop reachability affect whether backup routing activates.

q: What is a host route?
a: A host route matches one IP address, using /32 in IPv4 or /128 in IPv6.
why: Host routes are more specific than ordinary network routes containing the same address.

q: What happens to the IPv4 TTL when a router forwards a packet?
a: The router decrements the TTL by one and discards the packet if the resulting value is zero.
why: TTL helps prevent packets from circulating indefinitely.

q: What does traceroute help identify?
a: Traceroute helps reveal responding intermediate routers along a packet path using controlled hop limits.
why: Missing replies do not necessarily indicate a failed network hop.

q: What is OSPF?
a: Open Shortest Path First is a link-state interior gateway routing protocol that calculates shortest paths using a link-state database.
why: OSPFv2 is commonly used for IPv4 and OSPFv3 for IPv6.

q: What is an OSPF router ID?
a: An OSPF router ID is a 32-bit identifier represented in dotted-decimal format that identifies a router within an OSPF routing domain.
why: A router ID is not required to be a reachable IPv4 interface address.

q: What is the backbone OSPF area number?
a: Area 0 is the OSPF backbone area.
why: Single-area OSPF designs commonly place all participating interfaces into area 0.

q: Which Cisco command enables OSPFv2 on an interface in area 0?
a: The interface-level ip ospf process-id area 0 command activates OSPFv2 for that interface.
why: The OSPF process ID is locally significant.

q: What does OSPF Full neighbor state mean?
a: Full indicates that the OSPF neighbors have completed their required database synchronization.
why: On broadcast networks, some non-DR neighbors may remain at 2-Way normally.

q: What commonly prevents two OSPF routers from becoming neighbors?
a: Causes include area mismatch, incompatible hello/dead timers, network issues, duplicate router IDs, or incompatible OSPF parameters.
why: Check interface-level OSPF settings rather than relying only on IP reachability.

q: What is an OSPF designated router?
a: A designated router coordinates certain link-state exchanges on OSPF multiaccess networks and reduces adjacency overhead.
why: Broadcast networks elect a DR and BDR; point-to-point links do not require them.

q: How is an OSPF DR selected?
a: The highest eligible interface priority wins; router ID breaks ties among eligible routers.
why: OSPF DR elections are not normally preemptive.

q: What does OSPF passive-interface do?
a: It prevents OSPF neighbor formation on the selected interface while allowing its connected network to be advertised when appropriate.
why: Passive interfaces are useful on user-facing networks without OSPF neighbors.

q: Which command displays OSPFv2 neighbors?
a: The show ip ospf neighbor command lists discovered OSPFv2 neighbors and their adjacency states.
why: Look at neighbor state, router ID, and interface.

q: What is OSPFv3 used for in CCNA?
a: OSPFv3 is used to exchange IPv6 routing information and establish IPv6 routing adjacencies.
cli:
ipv6 unicast-routing
ipv6 router ospf 1
 router-id 1.1.1.1
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ipv6 ospf 1 area 0
why: This is classic IOS-style syntax; IOS XE may use router ospfv3 with address-family configuration.

q: What is HSRP?
a: Hot Standby Router Protocol provides gateway redundancy through a shared virtual IP address and an active/standby router arrangement.
why: Hosts use the virtual gateway rather than depending on one physical router.

q: What is VRRP?
a: Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol provides a virtual default gateway shared by participating routers, with a master and backup operation model.
why: VRRP is standardized, whereas HSRP originated with Cisco.

q: What is the default administrative distance of a connected route on Cisco IOS?
a: A directly connected route normally has an administrative distance of 0.
why: A connected route is strongly preferred when it is operational and matches the prefix.

q: What is DHCP?
a: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol automatically provides clients with IP configuration such as an address, subnet mask, gateway, and DNS servers.
why: DHCP does not guarantee the same address forever unless a reservation or other policy applies.

q: What are the four main DHCPv4 lease steps?
a: The common initial exchange is Discover, Offer, Request, and Acknowledge.
why: DHCPv4 clients typically use UDP ports 68 and 67.

q: What does ip helper-address do?
a: On Cisco IOS, ip helper-address can relay eligible UDP broadcasts, including DHCPv4 client messages, to a configured remote server.
why: DHCP broadcasts normally do not cross router interfaces without a relay mechanism.

q: How do you define a DHCPv4 address pool on Cisco IOS?
a: Create an ip dhcp pool and configure the network plus any necessary gateway and DNS options.
cli:
ip dhcp pool USERS
network 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0
default-router 192.168.10.1
dns-server 192.168.10.53
why: Exclude addresses that should not be leased dynamically.

q: What is DNS?
a: Domain Name System is a distributed naming service that resolves domain names and provides other information stored in DNS records.
why: DNS resolution failure can break name-based access even when IP connectivity works.

q: What does an A DNS record contain?
a: An A record associates a domain name with an IPv4 address.
why: An AAAA record is used for IPv6 addresses.

q: What does an AAAA DNS record contain?
a: An AAAA record associates a domain name with an IPv6 address.
why: Four A characters do not mean four different IPv4 addresses.

q: What is a CNAME DNS record?
a: A CNAME record makes one DNS name an alias for another canonical domain name.
why: A CNAME normally cannot coexist with other record types at the same owner name.

q: What does an MX DNS record identify?
a: An MX record identifies mail-exchange hosts responsible for accepting email for a domain, with preference values.
why: MX records point to hostnames, not directly to IP addresses.

q: What is the purpose of an NS record?
a: An NS record identifies an authoritative name server for a DNS zone or delegated namespace.
why: NS records are different from resolver configuration on a client.

q: What is a PTR record?
a: A PTR record maps a reverse-DNS name associated with an IP address to a hostname.
why: Reverse DNS does not automatically prove a host's identity.

q: Which transport port does DNS commonly use?
a: DNS commonly uses UDP port 53, while TCP port 53 is also used for DNS operations and larger or otherwise suitable exchanges.
why: DNS is not exclusively UDP.

q: What is NAT?
a: Network Address Translation changes IP address information as packets cross a translation device.
why: NAT is not itself a replacement for firewall policy.

q: What is PAT?
a: Port Address Translation allows multiple internal sessions to share translated IP addressing by distinguishing flows through transport identifiers such as port numbers.
why: PAT is often called NAT overload on Cisco devices.

q: Which Cisco command enables interface-based PAT?
a: After defining inside/outside interfaces and the matching ACL, use ip nat inside source list with the outside interface and overload keyword.
cli:
access-list 1 permit 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255
ip nat inside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/1 overload
why: The inside and outside interface NAT roles must also be configured.

q: Which Cisco command displays active NAT translations?
a: The show ip nat translations command lists current IPv4 NAT translation entries.
why: A missing translation may indicate no matching traffic or a configuration issue.

q: What is the default TCP port for SSH?
a: SSH normally uses TCP port 22 to provide encrypted remote access.
why: Telnet commonly uses TCP 23 and does not provide equivalent built-in encryption.

q: What is the difference between SCP and SFTP?
a: SCP supports secure file copying, while SFTP provides an SSH-based file-transfer protocol with richer file-management operations.
why: Both normally use SSH transport, but they are different protocols.

q: What is the purpose of NTP?
a: Network Time Protocol synchronizes device clocks with time sources across a network.
why: Accurate timestamps improve log correlation during troubleshooting.

q: What is SNMP?
a: Simple Network Management Protocol allows management systems to read device information and receive event notifications from compatible network devices.
why: SNMPv3 can provide authentication and privacy protection.

q: Which UDP ports are commonly used for SNMP?
a: SNMP commonly uses UDP 161 for agent queries and UDP 162 for traps or notifications.
why: A trap is an unsolicited notification, unlike an ordinary manager query.

q: What is syslog?
a: Syslog is a standardized approach for generating and transporting event messages used for monitoring and troubleshooting.
why: Cisco syslog messages include facility and severity information.

q: Which syslog severity is Emergency?
a: Syslog severity 0 represents Emergency, the most severe standard level.
why: Severity 7 is Debugging, the least severe standard level.

q: Which TCP port is commonly used for HTTPS?
a: HTTPS normally uses TCP port 443; HTTP/3 commonly uses UDP port 443.
why: HTTPS does not guarantee the website itself is trustworthy.

q: What is the CIA triad?
a: The CIA triad describes three information-security goals: Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability.
why: Integrity concerns unauthorized alteration, not simply keeping information secret.

q: What is AAA?
a: AAA is a framework for Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting in access management.
why: Authentication verifies identity; authorization determines permitted actions.

q: What is TACACS+?
a: TACACS+ is a network access-control protocol commonly used for centralized administration of network devices.
why: TACACS+ commonly uses TCP 49 and supports granular command authorization.

q: What is RADIUS?
a: RADIUS is a centralized AAA protocol commonly used for network access authentication and accounting.
why: RADIUS commonly uses UDP 1812 for authentication and 1813 for accounting.

q: What is an ACL?
a: An Access Control List is an ordered set of rules used to permit or deny matching network traffic or management access.
why: Traditional Cisco IPv4 ACLs include an implicit deny at the end.

q: What does a standard IPv4 ACL normally match?
a: A standard IPv4 ACL normally matches packets based on their source IPv4 address.
why: A standard ACL cannot directly match a destination TCP port.

q: What can an extended IPv4 ACL match?
a: An extended ACL can match source and destination addresses, protocols, and applicable transport-layer ports.
why: Extended ACLs are useful for more precise traffic filtering.

q: What is the implicit deny in a Cisco ACL?
a: An unmatched packet is denied after all applicable ACL entries have been evaluated.
why: Include explicit permit entries for traffic that must pass.

q: In what order does a Cisco ACL evaluate entries?
a: Entries are evaluated in sequence until the first matching rule determines the action.
why: A broad early permit or deny can prevent later entries from being reached.

q: How do you apply an IPv4 ACL to an interface?
a: Use ip access-group with the ACL identifier and the inbound or outbound direction.
why: Direction is evaluated relative to the interface, not the original application's viewpoint.

q: What is switch port security?
a: Port security restricts which source MAC addresses may use a protected Layer 2 access interface.
cli:
interface GigabitEthernet0/5
switchport mode access
switchport port-security
why: Port security is not a substitute for complete endpoint authentication.

q: What does sticky MAC learning do?
a: Sticky MAC learning adds dynamically observed secure MAC addresses to the running configuration as sticky secure addresses.
why: Save the configuration if sticky entries must persist across reloads.

q: What is the default port-security violation mode on many Cisco switches?
a: Shutdown is the common default, placing a violating interface into an error-disabled condition.
why: Protect, restrict, and shutdown handle violations differently.

q: What is DHCP snooping?
a: DHCP snooping is a Layer 2 security feature that examines DHCP traffic and helps prevent unauthorized DHCP server messages.
why: Trusted ports normally lead toward legitimate DHCP servers or relays.

q: Which command marks a DHCP snooping interface as trusted?
a: Use ip dhcp snooping trust on the appropriate interface.
cli:
interface GigabitEthernet0/24
ip dhcp snooping trust
why: Do not blindly trust unverified user-facing ports.

q: What is Dynamic ARP Inspection?
a: Dynamic ARP Inspection validates ARP packets against trusted binding information to reduce certain ARP-spoofing attacks.
why: DAI commonly relies on DHCP snooping bindings or configured ARP ACLs.

q: What is storm control?
a: Storm control limits specified traffic classes on a switch port when incoming broadcast, multicast, or unknown-unicast traffic exceeds configured thresholds.
why: It helps reduce disruption from excessive Layer 2 traffic.

q: What is IPv6 RA Guard?
a: RA Guard filters unauthorized IPv6 Router Advertisement messages on supported Layer 2 switch ports.
why: Rogue advertisements can influence IPv6 host gateway and prefix configuration.

q: What is an IPsec VPN?
a: An IPsec VPN uses IP-layer security protocols and negotiated keys to protect IP communication across an untrusted network.
why: IPsec designs may provide encryption, integrity, authentication, and anti-replay protection.

q: What is the difference between IPsec tunnel and transport modes?
a: Tunnel mode protects an encapsulated IP packet and adds a new outer IP header; transport mode generally protects the payload of the original IP packet.
why: Site-to-site IPsec VPNs commonly use tunnel mode.

q: What does IPsec ESP provide?
a: Encapsulating Security Payload can provide encryption, integrity, origin authentication, and anti-replay protection according to the negotiated settings.
why: ESP is not identical to the older IPsec Authentication Header protocol.

q: Why is SSH preferred over Telnet?
a: SSH protects remote-management sessions with encryption and integrity checks, while ordinary Telnet sends information without comparable cryptographic protection.
why: Use strong credentials and appropriate access controls even when SSH is enabled.

q: What does the principle of least privilege mean?
a: Users and services should receive only the permissions required for their authorized tasks.
why: Excessive privilege increases the impact of compromised credentials.

q: What is the difference between IDS and IPS?
a: An IDS primarily detects and reports suspicious activity, while an IPS can inspect and block traffic according to security policy.
why: An inline IPS may affect traffic availability if rules generate false positives.

q: What is a WLAN?
a: A Wireless Local Area Network connects compatible devices within a local network using wireless technologies such as Wi-Fi.
why: Wireless LANs still commonly connect to wired switching infrastructure.

q: What is a wireless access point?
a: A wireless access point provides radio connectivity for wireless clients and normally bridges their traffic into a network.
why: An AP and a router may be separate devices or combined in one home gateway.

q: What is an SSID?
a: A Service Set Identifier is the name used to identify a Wi-Fi network.
why: An SSID is not itself a security mechanism.

q: What is a BSSID?
a: A Basic Service Set Identifier identifies an individual Wi-Fi basic service set and commonly corresponds to an AP radio's virtual MAC address.
why: Multiple APs can advertise the same SSID while using different BSSIDs.
imgAlt: Real Cisco Aironet 1100 wireless access point

q: What is an ESS?
a: An Extended Service Set combines multiple infrastructure basic service sets into a broader WLAN service, commonly sharing an SSID.
why: An ESS helps support coverage and roaming across multiple APs.

q: Which three 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi channels are commonly nonoverlapping in 20 MHz channel plans?
a: Channels 1, 6, and 11 are commonly used as nonoverlapping 20 MHz channels in regulatory domains that support them.
why: Actual permitted channels depend on local regulations.

q: What is a common advantage of 5 GHz Wi-Fi over 2.4 GHz?
a: The 5 GHz band generally provides more available channel options and often experiences less congestion from 2.4 GHz devices.
why: Higher frequencies often experience greater loss through obstacles.

q: What is Wi-Fi 6?
a: Wi-Fi 6 refers to IEEE 802.11ax technology, designed to improve wireless efficiency and capacity.
why: Wi-Fi 6E extends supported 802.11ax operation into the 6 GHz band.

q: What IEEE standard underlies Wi-Fi 7?
a: Wi-Fi 7 is based on IEEE 802.11be and introduces features such as multi-link operation.
why: Wi-Fi 7 capabilities depend on client, AP, spectrum, and regional support.

q: What is RF interference?
a: RF interference is unwanted electromagnetic energy that degrades wireless signal reception or communication performance.
why: Interference can come from neighboring Wi-Fi networks or non-Wi-Fi transmitters.

q: What does RSSI indicate?
a: Received Signal Strength Indicator is a measure of received radio signal power or strength, often reported using vendor-specific scales.
why: Signal strength alone does not describe signal-to-noise ratio or throughput.

q: What does SNR mean in wireless networking?
a: Signal-to-Noise Ratio compares useful received signal power with background noise power.
why: A higher SNR generally supports more reliable high-rate communication.

q: What is WPA2-Personal?
a: WPA2-Personal is a Wi-Fi security mode that commonly uses a shared passphrase to derive authentication and encryption keys.
why: Strong passphrases help resist offline guessing attacks against captured handshakes.

q: What is WPA3-Personal?
a: WPA3-Personal uses Simultaneous Authentication of Equals, or SAE, for password-based authentication.
why: WPA3-Personal differs from WPA2-PSK's traditional four-way-handshake authentication model.

q: What does WPA-Enterprise commonly use for authentication?
a: WPA-Enterprise commonly uses IEEE 802.1X authentication with EAP and a backend authentication service such as RADIUS.
why: Enterprise Wi-Fi can use individual user or device credentials instead of one shared passphrase.

q: What is a wireless LAN controller?
a: A WLC centrally manages supported access points and wireless network configurations.
why: Controller-managed APs may use CAPWAP for management and control.

q: What is CAPWAP?
a: Control and Provisioning of Wireless Access Points is a protocol framework used between compatible APs and wireless controllers.
why: CAPWAP control traffic commonly uses UDP 5246.

q: A Wi-Fi client sees an SSID but cannot connect. What should be checked first?
a: Check the configured security mode, credentials, client compatibility, signal conditions, and authentication or association failure information.
why: Seeing an SSID does not guarantee successful authentication or IP configuration.

q: What is network automation?
a: Network automation uses software-controlled processes to perform networking tasks such as configuration, validation, and monitoring with reduced manual repetition.
why: Automated changes still require approval, validation, and rollback planning.

q: What is infrastructure as code?
a: Infrastructure as Code defines infrastructure resources and desired configurations in machine-readable files managed through software workflows.
why: Version control and review help manage infrastructure changes.

q: What is a hypervisor?
a: A hypervisor is software or firmware that creates and manages virtual machines by abstracting underlying hardware resources.
why: Virtual machines can run separate guest operating systems on shared hardware.

q: What is a container?
a: A container packages an application and its dependencies in an isolated environment that commonly shares the host operating-system kernel.
why: A container does not normally require its own complete guest operating system.

q: What is a REST API?
a: A REST API exposes resources through a network interface using HTTP methods and stateless request-response interactions.
why: Not every HTTP API fully follows REST architectural constraints.

q: What does an HTTP GET request normally do?
a: GET requests a representation of a resource without intending to modify server state.
why: GET should be safe and idempotent under HTTP semantics.

q: What does an HTTP POST request commonly do?
a: POST submits data for processing and can create resources or trigger operations depending on the API.
why: POST is not generally guaranteed to be idempotent.

q: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
a: PUT defines a replacement representation for a target resource, while PATCH applies a set of partial modifications.
why: PUT is defined as idempotent; PATCH is not inherently idempotent.

q: What does HTTP status 200 mean?
a: HTTP 200 OK indicates that the request succeeded.
why: A successful resource creation may return 201 instead.

q: What does HTTP status 401 mean?
a: HTTP 401 Unauthorized indicates that valid authentication credentials are required or were not accepted.
why: HTTP 403 means the server understood the request but refuses to fulfill it.

q: What is JSON?
a: JavaScript Object Notation is a structured text format that represents data using objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null.
why: JSON objects use quoted property names and do not permit trailing commas.

q: What is YAML?
a: YAML is a human-readable data serialization format commonly used for automation configuration and declarative files.
why: Indentation is significant in YAML.

q: What is XML?
a: Extensible Markup Language is a text-based format that represents structured data using elements and attributes.
why: NETCONF commonly uses XML-encoded messages.

q: What is a control plane?
a: The control plane runs protocols and processes that establish network state and determine forwarding behavior.
why: Routing protocols are part of control-plane operation.

q: What is a data plane?
a: The data plane forwards packets or frames according to installed forwarding information and policies.
why: The control plane determines forwarding information; the data plane applies it.

q: What is controller-based networking?
a: Controller-based networking centralizes aspects of network policy, configuration, or control through a controller or management platform.
why: Centralized control does not necessarily mean all packet forwarding occurs at the controller.

q: What is Ansible?
a: Ansible is an automation platform that executes tasks and manages configurations using inventories, modules, and playbooks.
why: Many network-device workflows use APIs or remote CLI connections rather than requiring an agent on the device.

q: What does an Ansible inventory contain?
a: An inventory identifies managed hosts or groups and may define connection and configuration variables.
why: Separate sensitive credentials from publicly shared inventory files.

q: What is an Ansible playbook?
a: A playbook is a YAML document describing ordered automation plays and tasks to run against selected systems.
why: Tasks should be designed for predictable and repeatable execution.

q: Which Ansible module can run Cisco IOS show commands?
a: The cisco.ios.ios_command module can execute supported IOS CLI commands through a suitable network connection.
cli:
- name: Read interface status
  cisco.ios.ios_command:
    commands:
      - show ip interface brief
why: Ensure the appropriate Cisco collection and connection plugin are available.

q: What does idempotence mean in automation?
a: An idempotent operation produces the same intended state when repeated without additional unintended changes.
why: Idempotent configuration tasks are safer to rerun.

q: What is agentic AI in network operations?
a: Agentic AI can plan and perform multi-step operational tasks using tools and feedback under defined permissions and controls.
why: AI-generated actions require authorization, safeguards, and verification before production use.

q: What should a safe AI networking troubleshooting prompt include?
a: It should specify the network context, authorized task, sanitized evidence, constraints, and required output format.
why: Avoid exposing credentials or sensitive production data in prompts.

q: What is an important verification step after an automated network change?
a: Compare intended configuration with actual state and test relevant connectivity, service health, and expected policy behavior.
why: A successful automation run does not by itself prove that network service works correctly.

q: What does a router use to forward packets?
a: Destination IP addresses and its routing table.
why: Routers examine the destination IP and select a matching route to the next network.
imgAlt: Real Cisco 1800 series routers stacked above Cisco Ethernet switches in a physical networking lab

q: Why does STP block redundant Layer 2 paths?
a: To prevent switching loops, broadcast storms, and MAC table instability.
why: STP provides a loop-free active topology while keeping some redundant links available for failover.
imgAlt: Original technical diagram for Spanning Tree

q: What must OSPF neighbors do before exchanging routes?
a: Establish an adjacency and synchronize their link-state databases.
why: They exchange Hello messages to discover neighbors; eligible adjacencies progress toward Full.

q: How does PAT distinguish simultaneous sessions?
a: It uses translated IP addresses and transport-layer ports or other protocol identifiers.
why: Many inside hosts can share one public IPv4 address while their sessions remain distinguishable.

q: What is the difference between SSID and BSSID?
a: SSID names a Wi-Fi network; BSSID identifies a specific basic service set.
why: Multiple AP radios can advertise the same SSID while using different BSSIDs.

q: PC 10.8.4.130/25: what is its network address?
why: A /25 splits the last octet into .0–.127 and .128–.255. Address .130 falls in the second block.
Both match, but /25 is more specific than /24. Longest-prefix matching applies before route preference.

q: An unknown unicast frame arrives in VLAN 20. What happens?
a: The switch floods it to other forwarding ports in VLAN 20, excluding ingress.
why: Flooding stays within the VLAN; a different VLAN does not receive the frame through normal Layer 2 switching.
imgAlt: Real Cisco Catalyst Ethernet switch ports

q: A PC in VLAN 10 must reach VLAN 20. What is required?
a: Layer 3 routing through a router or multilayer switch.
why: VLANs are separate Layer 2 broadcast domains. Switching alone cannot move IP packets between them.

q: Which IOS command verifies learned switch MAC entries?
a: show mac address-table
why: It displays learned MAC addresses with associated VLANs and interfaces on supported Cisco switches.
imgAlt: Real Cisco Catalyst Ethernet switch ports

q: OSPF neighbors stay in INIT. What does that suggest?
a: The router receives Hellos but does not see its own router ID in them.
why: A 2-Way state requires bidirectional recognition. Check neighbor reachability and Hello content.

q: A PC has 169.254.8.12. What likely failed?
a: It could not obtain an IPv4 lease through DHCP and self-assigned a link-local address.
why: Check the client VLAN, DHCP server, pool, relay configuration, and connectivity.
cli:
IPv4 Address: 169.254.8.12
Subnet Mask: 255.255.0.0
Default Gateway: (none)

q: A host pings its gateway but cannot resolve example.com. What should you test next?
a: Test DNS resolution, for example with nslookup example.com.
why: Gateway reachability alone does not verify Internet connectivity; a DNS lookup isolates name-resolution issues.

q: Which address is used for next-hop communication on many IPv6 LAN links?
a: A link-local IPv6 address (fe80::/10).
why: IPv6 routing protocols and default gateways commonly use link-local next-hop addresses on a local link.

q: What type of network connector is shown?
a: An 8P8C modular plug commonly used for Ethernet.
why: People often call it RJ45. The eight contacts carry Ethernet signals over twisted-pair cabling.

q: Which device in the picture connects local Ethernet hosts?
a: A network switch.
why: A Layer 2 switch forwards frames toward the correct port using learned MAC addresses.
imgAlt: Actual Cisco Catalyst 4006 Ethernet switch port banks (not a router)

q: What path does the picture illustrate?
a: PC → switch → router → remote server.
why: Switches forward local Ethernet frames; routers forward packets between IP networks.
imgAlt: Original technical diagram for Network Basics

q: What does a switch port LED generally help show?
a: Link status or activity; exact meanings depend on the model.
why: An unlit link indicator can point to cabling, power, or interface problems.
imgAlt: Real Cisco Catalyst Ethernet switch ports

q: What does S* 0.0.0.0/0 mean in a routing table?
a: A candidate default route selected from a static route.
why: S means static. The asterisk indicates a candidate default route.
cli:
Gateway of last resort is 10.0.0.1 to network 0.0.0.0
S* 0.0.0.0/0 [1/0] via 10.0.0.1

q: What does VLAN 20 in this MAC table entry tell you?
a: The MAC address was learned in VLAN 20.
why: MAC forwarding decisions are scoped to the VLAN, not the entire switch.
cli:
Vlan    Mac Address       Type       Ports
  20    0011.2233.4455    DYNAMIC    Fa0/5

q: What neighbor state shows a usable OSPF adjacency?
a: FULL.
why: FULL means the routers have synchronized link-state databases for their adjacency.
cli:
Neighbor ID     Pri  State       Dead Time   Address
2.2.2.2           1  FULL/DR     00:00:35    10.0.12.2

q: What is the effect of the final implicit ACL rule?
a: Packets not matched by an earlier permit are denied.
why: ACLs are evaluated top to bottom; the first matching ACE determines the action.
cli:
ip access-list extended WEB-FILTER
 permit tcp 10.0.10.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 443
 deny ip any any log

q: What does DHCP snooping build for downstream checks?
a: A binding table mapping DHCP-learned IP, MAC, VLAN, and interface.
why: Dynamic ARP Inspection can use trusted DHCP snooping bindings to check ARP traffic.

q: What file format do Ansible playbooks commonly use?
a: YAML.
why: Playbooks define tasks and host groups in human-readable structured data.

q: Which tool view helps inspect frame fields and bytes?
a: Wireshark packet details and packet bytes panes.
why: Select a packet, expand its protocol layers, and inspect the raw bytes below.
imgAlt: Genuine Wireshark main window showing a selected DNS response, packet details, and packet bytes
imgCredit: Wireshark project, documentation image · see project documentation licensing

q: What does this command verify?
a: The operational status and membership of EtherChannel groups.
why: Check P flags for bundled ports and SU for a Layer 2 port-channel in use.
cli:
Switch# show etherchannel summary
Group  Port-channel  Protocol  Ports
1      Po1(SU)       LACP      Gi0/1(P) Gi0/2(P)

q: 192.168.10.142/27: network address?
why: /27 blocks are 32: 128–159 contains 142.

q: How many usable hosts in a conventional /29 subnet?
why: There are 8 total IPv4 addresses; network and broadcast use two.

q: 10.10.8.10 matches /16, /24, /28 routes. Which wins?
a: The longest matching prefix: /28, if the /28 includes 10.10.8.10.
why: Routing chooses the most specific matching prefix before AD or metric.

q: A PC is in VLAN 20, but port Fa0/7 is assigned to VLAN 10. First fix?
a: Put Fa0/7 in VLAN 20 after verifying the intended VLAN and host design.
why: Access VLAN mismatch places the host in the wrong broadcast domain.

q: SW1 learns MAC A on Fa0/1. A moves to Fa0/9. What changes?
a: The MAC table entry updates to the new ingress port.
why: Source MAC learning moves the entry when frames arrive on the new port.

q: OSPF neighbors stuck in EXSTART: where would you investigate?
a: Check MTU mismatches and adjacency negotiation issues.
why: Mismatched MTU is a common cause; also inspect master/slave negotiation and logs.

q: ACL permits 10.0.0.0/24. Does 10.0.1.15 match?
a: No.

q: Clients on VLAN 30 get no DHCP leases; server is in another VLAN. Check?
a: Check the VLAN 30 gateway interface and DHCP relay (ip helper-address).
why: DHCP broadcasts need a relay to reach a remote server.

q: Inside host reaches public IP but PAT return packets fail. Verify first?
a: Inspect NAT translations, ACL match, inside/outside interfaces, and routes.
why: A wrong NAT direction, rule, or missing route can break return flows.

q: An unauthorized DHCP offer appears on an access port. Best defense?
a: Enable DHCP snooping and trust only legitimate DHCP-facing ports.
why: Untrusted ports drop server-side DHCP messages.

q: Which connected network exists in this routing table?
a: 192.168.10.0/24 directly connected on GigabitEthernet0/0.
why: C marks connected networks and L marks local host routes.
cli:
C 192.168.10.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
L 192.168.10.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0

q: Before running an AI-suggested configuration, what should you do?
a: Validate commands, scope, evidence, risks, and obtain authorized approval.
why: Generated advice is not verified device state. Review before execution.

q: Clients on 2.4 GHz suffer interference; what should you inspect?
a: Channel usage, overlap, signal levels, and competing RF sources.
why: Prefer nonoverlapping 20 MHz channels where applicable and verify local RF conditions.

q: What could cause DAI to drop valid ARP replies?
a: Missing or incorrect DHCP snooping bindings or ARP ACLs.
why: DAI validates ARP on untrusted ports; static IP hosts may require ARP ACLs.
cli:
Switch# show ip arp inspection statistics
Vlan  Forwarded  Dropped  DHCP Drops
10    225        86       86

q: Explain a VLAN in 20 seconds.
a: A VLAN separates one physical switching environment into logical Layer 2 networks. Inter-VLAN traffic needs routing.
why: Mention a real use: isolate staff and student access ports.

q: A user cannot reach the internet. What do you check first?
a: Check link/Wi-Fi, IP and mask, gateway, DNS, then upstream connectivity and policy.
why: Use a layered approach and state what each test proves.

q: Walk me through troubleshooting a wrong VLAN.
a: Check the assigned access VLAN, trunk allowance, VLAN existence, IP subnet, and Layer 3 gateway.
why: Distinguish a VLAN membership issue from an IP addressing issue.

q: Explain a packet going between two networks.
a: The host sends a frame to its gateway MAC. The router selects a route and re-encapsulates for the next hop.
why: IP destination usually remains unchanged unless NAT applies; L2 headers change.

q: What would you do after a network change caused an outage?
a: Confirm impact, compare changes, check evidence, roll back safely, then verify service.
why: A strong answer includes communication, approvals, and a recovery check.

q: Explain why subnetting matters to a company.
a: It plans address space, limits Layer 2 broadcast scope, and supports segmentation and routing.
why: Avoid claiming subnetting alone is a security boundary.

q: Explain OSPF neighbor establishment.
a: Routers discover neighbors with Hellos and synchronize link-state data where adjacency is required.
why: Mention area, timers, subnet, and MTU as troubleshooting checks.

q: How would you verify a new trunk?
a: Check switchport mode, allowed VLANs, native VLAN, neighbor link, and test traffic.
why: Use show interfaces trunk and show interfaces switchport on Cisco IOS.

q: When would you use Wireshark?
a: To inspect packet-level behavior such as DNS errors, TCP handshakes, and retransmissions.
why: Use authorized captures, relevant filters, and protect sensitive data.
imgAlt: Genuine Wireshark main window showing a selected DNS response, packet details, and packet bytes
imgCredit: Wireshark project, documentation image · see project documentation licensing

q: How would you explain a default route?
a: A less-specific route used when no more-specific destination route matches.
why: Describe a small branch sending unknown destinations to its upstream router.

q: Which connector is shown: RJ45 Ethernet or LC fiber?
a: RJ45-style 8P8C modular plug used for twisted-pair Ethernet connections.
why: RJ45 connectors have eight contact positions; fiber connectors have a different shape.

q: What are these optical connectors called: LC or SC?
a: The smaller connector is LC, while the larger connector is SC.
why: Connector type, fiber mode, and transceiver specifications must be compatible.
imgAlt: Real LC and SC fiber-optic connectors

q: What networking component is pictured in this close-up?
a: An SFP optical transceiver module, which fits a compatible SFP slot and connects the network device to optical media.
why: SFP and SFP+ specifications are not interchangeable by name alone.

q: What type of wireless networking device is shown?
a: A Cisco Aironet wireless access point that provides Wi-Fi access to a local network.
why: An AP is not necessarily a router or the default gateway.
imgAlt: Real Cisco Aironet 1100 wireless access point

q: In this photo, identify the routers and switches.
a: The two upper teal Cisco 1800-series devices are routers; the lower port-dense devices are Ethernet switches.
why: A device’s physical ports and model identify its role more reliably than cable color.
imgAlt: Real Cisco 1800 series routers stacked above Cisco Ethernet switches in a physical networking lab
